content.title: About
content.content: Reduced‑fat cheddar is a semi‑hard cheese made from cow’s milk in which a portion of the cream is removed or replaced with skim milk. It retains the sharp, tangy flavor of traditional cheddar while providing fewer calories and less saturated fat.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cheddar originated in the English village of Cheddar in the 12th century and is now one of the world’s most popular cheeses.
Fat reduction is achieved by separating part of the milk fat after curd formation.
The cheese is aged from 3 to 12 months; longer aging intensifies the flavor.
Reduced‑fat cheddar is favored in diet‑focused meals where cheese texture is desired without the full calorie load.
It melts well, making it a common choice for sauces, casseroles, and pizza.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Provides about 700 mg of calcium per 100 g, supporting bone and teeth health.

items.title: Good source of protein
items.content: Delivers roughly 25 g of high‑quality protein, essential for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains vitamin B12
items.content: Vitamin B12 aids nerve function and red blood cell formation.

items.title: Lower saturated fat
items.content: Reduced fat content makes it more suitable for diets limiting saturated fats.

items.title: Probiotic potential
items.content: Like other fermented cheeses, cheddar contains live cultures that can benefit gut microbiota.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: The cheese still contains lactose; individuals with intolerance should limit intake.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Some people may react to casein, the main milk protein.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Cheddar can be salty; those with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Despite reduced fat, it remains calorie‑dense; moderation is key.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Reduced‑fat cheddar works well sliced for sandwiches, cubed in salads, grated for sauces, casseroles, and pizza. It can also be enjoyed as a snack on its own.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep in its original packaging or an airtight container in the refrigerator at 1‑4 °C. It stays fresh for up to 4 weeks. If mold appears, cut away the affected area and use the remaining cheese.

pasta-with-cream-sauce-poultry-and-added.title: Pasta with Cream Sauce, Poultry and Vegetables

content.title: About
content.content: A home‑cooked pasta dish featuring a smooth cream sauce, bite‑size pieces of chicken breast and a mix of vegetables (carrot, broccoli, bell pepper). The pasta supplies quick‑release carbs, while the chicken and veggies add protein, vitamins and minerals.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cream sauce is often made with a roux of flour and low‑fat cream, making it lighter than classic Alfredo.
Chicken breast is one of the leanest meats, low in fat and high in high‑quality protein.
Broccoli is rich in vitamin C and phytochemicals that support the body’s detox pathways.
Cooking pasta al dente preserves its texture and lowers its glycemic impact.
A homemade recipe lets you control salt levels and add favorite herbs such as basil or paprika.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken breast provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: The vegetables contribute vitamins A, C, K and minerals like potassium and magnesium, supporting immunity and heart health.

items.title: Energy supply
items.content: Pasta delivers carbohydrates that are rapidly converted to energy, especially useful after physical activity.

items.title: Digestive support
items.content: Fiber from the vegetables aids gut motility and promotes satiety.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: Using low‑fat cream keeps the overall saturated‑fat content of the dish modest.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cream can trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk‑protein allergy.

items.title: Undercooked poultry
items.content: Insufficiently cooked chicken may harbor harmful bacteria; ensure an internal temperature of 75 °C.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Added salt in the sauce can increase sodium intake; use it sparingly.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: The cream sauce adds calories, so portion control is advisable for weight‑management diets.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pasta hot, tossed with the sauce, chicken and vegetables. Garnish with fresh basil, grated Parmesan or a pinch of black pepper for extra flavor. The dish keeps well in the fridge for up to 2 days and can be reheated in a microwave or skillet.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the leftovers in an airtight container and refrigerate for no more than 48 hours. For longer storage, freeze in portion‑size bags for up to 3 months. Reheat to at least 75 °C before serving.

content.title: About
content.content: Brown rice is a whole‑grain rice that retains its bran layer and germ. When prepared with soy sauce it gains a savory, slightly salty flavor typical of Asian cuisine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Brown rice contains more fiber and nutrients than white rice because it is not polished.
Soy sauce is traditionally made by fermenting soybeans, wheat, salt and water.
In Japan brown rice is called “genmai”, while in China it is known as “huzhou”.
Stored properly, brown rice can stay fresh for up to six months.
The rice‑soy sauce combination is a staple in stir‑fry dishes and sushi rolls.

items.title: High in fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Source of magnesium
items.content: Magnesium aids normal muscle and nerve function and participates in energy metabolism.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: The bran of brown rice is rich in phenolic compounds that protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Compared with white rice, brown rice releases glucose more slowly, which is beneficial for weight management.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B3 and B6 are involved in carbohydrate metabolism and support the nervous system.

items.title: Arsenic content
items.content: Like many grains, brown rice can contain trace amounts of arsenic; rinsing the rice and rotating with other grains is recommended.

items.title: Sodium in soy sauce
items.content: Soy sauce is high in sodium, so people with hypertension should limit their portion.

items.title: Soy allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to soy products.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the rice as a side dish with meat, fish or vegetables, add it to salads, soups or stir‑fries. Cook it in a rice cooker or on the stovetop using a 2:1 water‑to‑rice ratio. Before serving, drizzle a modest amount of soy sauce over the cooked rice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep dry brown rice in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. Cooked rice should be cooled quickly and stored in the refrigerator for no more than 3‑4 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Greek yogurt made from whole milk is a thick, creamy yogurt obtained by extensive straining, which removes most of the whey. It has a rich, buttery flavor with a mild tang and a high protein content.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Greek yogurt, known as “straggisto” in Greece, has been a staple of the Mediterranean diet for centuries.
Straining makes it 2‑3 times thicker than regular yogurt.
Its high protein level makes it popular among athletes and fitness enthusiasts.
Unlike low‑fat versions, the whole‑milk product retains natural fats that aid absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.
Greek yogurt is often used as a substitute for sour cream or mayonnaise in recipes.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: A typical 200 g serving provides about 10‑12 g of high‑quality protein, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Contains live cultures of Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium that promote a healthy gut microbiome.

items.title: Source of calcium
items.content: Whole milk supplies a good amount of calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Provides vitamin B12 and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Satiety aid
items.content: The thick texture and protein content help keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Although some lactose is removed during straining, the product still contains enough to cause symptoms in lactose‑intolerant individuals.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or whey proteins may react to Greek yogurt.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Whole‑milk Greek yogurt contains roughly 120 kcal per 100 g, so portion control is advisable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some brands add salt; those monitoring sodium intake should check the label.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy it plain, blend into smoothies, use as a base for dips and dressings, or substitute for cream cheese in baking and cooking.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated at +2‑4 °C in the original container. Once opened, consume within 5‑7 days. Discard if it develops off‑odors, mold, or an unusual texture.
